The promised stone bears a name known to its recipient. The Catechism cites this verse when teaching that those who live in Christ retain, or rather find, their true identity. Communion fulfils individuality instead of erasing it. Revelation invites hope for a belonging deeper than the labels imposed by status, achievement or rejection. The name is received as a gift: personal uniqueness and complete communion can belong together in the life God gives.

CCC 1025

The second death names a loss beyond physical dying: definitive separation from God. Catholic teaching calls hell the self-exclusion of someone who dies in mortal sin without repentance. It also insists that God predestines no one to this end, and the Church prays for all to receive mercy. The warning honours the seriousness of freedom. It calls us to respond to life now, without claiming certainty about another person's final destiny.

CCC 1033 · CCC 1037

phrase: glory and honour of the nations
body:
The nations bring their glory into the city lit by God and the Lamb. The Catechism teaches that work done in the Spirit will be found again, purified and transformed. Earthly progress is distinct from God's kingdom, yet the promised renewal strengthens concern for this world. Justice, humane relationships and beauty need not be lost. Their final fulfilment belongs to God, so faithful work can matter beyond the results we presently see.

CCC 1049 · CCC 1050

The domination described here belongs to the disorder that follows sin. The Catechism places it alongside broken trust and harmony: it is something humanity needs healing from, not the original purpose of marriage. Genesis has already given man and woman the same divine image and a vocation to mutual help. Reading the judgement within that larger story prevents it becoming a religious warrant for coercion. Redemption calls relationships towards the communion for which they were made.

CCC 400

phrase: it grieved him in his heart
body:
Scripture speaks of God's grief so that the horror of human violence can be heard within a relationship. Augustine explains divine reconsideration as an unchanging wisdom bringing about change, rather than God discovering that he made a mistake. The image does not make cruelty a matter of indifference to God. It expresses his judgement in words human beings can understand, while his faithful purpose exceeds the instability of our moods.

Augustine, City of God 15.25

Noah's speech names Canaan, not every descendant of Ham, and says nothing about skin colour. It cannot supply a divine warrant for racial enslavement. Earlier in this chapter, humanity's dignity is grounded in God's image; Catholic teaching therefore rejects discrimination in fundamental rights on grounds of race or colour. The difficult family episode must be read within that larger moral horizon, not turned into a permanent hierarchy of human worth.

CCC 1934–1935

phrase: he loved also Rachel more than Leah
body:
Jacob's household belongs to a stage in the Bible's unfolding account of marriage. The Catechism notes that patriarchal polygamy is not yet explicitly rejected; understanding of marriage's unity develops through the Law and prophets, before Jesus recalls its original meaning. The rivalry and unequal affection here should not be mistaken for a model of Christian marriage. Scripture tells the history of people being drawn towards God's purpose, including arrangements that fall short of its fullness.

CCC 1610–1614.

phrase: she shall be unclean seven days
body:
'Unclean' here names a temporary ritual status, not a judgement that giving birth is morally wrong. The Catholic Encyclopedia distinguishes ceremonial uncleanness from moral guilt in Mosaic law. This chapter regulates access to the sanctuary after childbirth; its purification offering should be read within that setting. The distinction matters throughout Leviticus: a bodily condition or contact with something ritually unclean does not by itself show that a person has chosen evil.

CE, Clean and Unclean.

phrase: They shall surely be put to death
body:
This ancient death sentence is not a Christian mandate to execute anyone. Catholic teaching distinguishes its moral judgement about sexual acts from every person's enduring dignity. The Catechism requires respect, compassion and sensitivity towards people with same-sex attraction, rejecting unjust discrimination. It also judges the death penalty inadmissible. Reading this law within Catholic faith therefore cannot justify violence, humiliation or denial of anyone's humanity.

CCC 2357–2358 · CCC 2267.

phrase: kill every male amongst the little ones
body:
Moses commands the killing of children and captive women. The severity cannot be explained away as harmless symbolism. Catholic reading receives the Old Testament within God's preparation for Christ, while acknowledging its imperfect and provisional elements. That framework does not dissolve every difficulty in this passage. It does rule out using it as Christian permission for such acts: the Catechism requires humane treatment of noncombatants and prisoners, condemns extermination, and requires resistance to orders commanding genocide. Religious language does not exempt violence from moral judgement.

CCC 122; CCC 2313

This command treats departure from Israel's covenant as a capital offence, creating a real difficulty for Christian readers. It is not permission to kill someone for urging another religion. Catholic teaching insists that faith must be free and that religious liberty rests on personal dignity, including the dignity of those who fail to seek or follow truth. Respecting that freedom does not declare every belief true; it recognises that violence cannot produce the free assent faith requires.

CCC 160; CCC 2106–2108

phrase: to the lady you shall do nothing
body:
This law distinguishes an assault victim from someone who freely commits adultery. Its surrounding test about whether she cried out remains deeply problematic: silence does not establish consent. Fear and coercion can prevent free action. Catholic teaching condemns rape as a violation of another person's freedom and bodily integrity, while recognising that duress affects responsibility. A victim's failure to resist audibly must therefore never be treated as proof of willing participation or as a reason to withhold protection.

CCC 2356; CCC 1735

phrase: Now I know that the LORD will do good to me
body:
Micah assumes that employing a Levite secures God’s favour, although his household shrine contains idols. The confidence is part of the story’s disorder, not its judgement of sound worship. The Catechism calls it superstition when religious practices are treated as effective through external performance alone. A priest, sacred object or ceremony cannot make God our possession. Worship calls us to conversion; it does not purchase protection for whatever we already intend to do.

CCC 2111

Saul’s guards refuse the order to kill the priests. Their refusal exposes a limit that royal command cannot erase; Doeg’s compliance then makes the threatened violence real. The Catechism teaches that conscience forbids obeying civil directives contrary to the moral order, fundamental rights or the Gospel. Authority does not transfer responsibility away from the person acting. Here resistance begins with withholding the hand that power wants to use against others.

CCC 2242.

The dead man revives on touching Elisha’s bones. Cyril of Jerusalem reads this as evidence that holiness concerns the body as well as the soul: the prophet’s body had served his righteous life, and God’s work through it does not end at death. He compares the healing associated with Paul’s cloths in Acts 19. This patristic reading helps explain reverence for saints’ remains through the dignity of embodied holiness, with God as the giver of life.

Cyril, Catechetical Lecture 18.16.

phrase: on the wilderness, in which there is no man
body:
Rain nourishes a place where no human being lives to benefit from it. The question widens Job’s horizon: creation’s goodness is larger than its place in our immediate concerns. The Catechism affirms that each creature has its own particular goodness and reflects the Creator in its own way. The wilderness is not wasted simply because nobody harvests it. Respect for creation begins by recognising goods we did not make and cannot measure solely by their usefulness to us.

CCC 339

phrase: Against you, and you only, I have sinned
body:
The psalm’s heading recalls David’s wrongdoing involving Bathsheba, so ‘you only’ cannot mean that no human being was harmed. It places sin before God at its deepest level. The Catechism quotes this verse immediately after defining sin as a failure of love for both God and neighbour that injures human solidarity. Turning to God therefore includes facing what we have done to people. Confession seeks divine mercy without making the injured neighbour disappear from the work of repentance.

CCC 1849–1850

In the poem, Wisdom invites the inexperienced to a meal that represents learning how to live. Augustine receives this invitation sacramentally: the eternal Word has assumed a human body and furnishes a table of bread and wine, drawing the weak into his life. This Christian reading does not replace the literal invitation to wisdom. It deepens its image of nourishment: Christ teaches the way of life and gives himself to sustain those who follow it. Communion is a gift that also calls for growth in understanding.

Augustine, City of God XVII.20

phrase: Don’t withhold correction from a child
body:
The rod belongs to this proverb’s ancient setting; its purpose is to prevent a child’s ruin through neglect of formation. Catholic teaching places parental correction within respect for the child as a person, a home marked by tenderness and forgiveness, and parents’ willingness to admit their own failings. Authority serves growing freedom and sound judgement. The following assurance about survival is wisdom rhetoric, not a guarantee that physical punishment cannot injure. A child’s dignity sets the measure for how correction is given.

CCC 2222–2223

The next verse speaks of the dead no longer sharing in what happens ‘under the sun’. Ecclesiastes confronts death as the end of familiar earthly activity; it is not presenting the full Christian account of life beyond death. The Catechism describes resurrection hope as progressively revealed, reaching its centre in Christ. Read within that unfolding revelation, these stark words keep their force: our present opportunities are limited and should be received seriously. They need not become a denial of communion with God beyond the grave.

CCC 992–994

Sirach warns that aid may strengthen someone who will use it to harm the giver. That concern explains the surrounding advice, but its restriction to the deserving is not the final Christian measure of charity. The Catechism recognises provisional elements within the Old Testament’s divine teaching and affirms Christ’s command to love enemies. Discernment still matters: helping a person need not mean supplying the means for wrongdoing. Their need, however, cannot be dismissed simply because we judge them sinful.

CCC 122; CCC 1933

phrase: The beginning of sin came from a woman
body:
This severe saying recalls Eve within a passage warning men about a harmful wife. It must be read alongside the whole biblical account, in which both first parents disobey. Catholic teaching explicitly names Adam and Eve together and affirms the equal, inalienable dignity of women and men. Original sin describes humanity’s wounded condition; it does not make women a morally inferior class or personally responsible for everyone’s wrongdoing. The fall calls all of us to conversion, not one sex to bear the blame for the other.

CCC 404–405; CCC 369

This advice assumes an ancient slaveholding household. The later call to avoid injustice and treat a slave like oneself introduces restraint, but the coercion here remains real. Catholic teaching condemns enslavement and reducing persons to their productive value; it also rejects torture as contrary to human dignity. Reading the passage within that fuller moral understanding brings the enslaved person into view as a neighbour with rights, rather than a troublesome possession. Its ancient setting explains the advice without making it a Christian rule for treating another person.

CCC 2414; CCC 2297

This taunt addresses Babylon’s king, whose ambition to rise above the stars ends in the grave. The Latin name Lucifer was used for the brilliant morning star; here it renders the image of the fallen ruler. The Catholic Encyclopedia distinguishes that immediate meaning from the later Christian application to the devil’s fall. The image exposes pride that tries to occupy God’s place. Lucifer was not originally an exclusively evil name: Christian texts also use morning-star language positively, including for Christ.

CE, Lucifer.

The promise is addressed to a community in exile, with a seventy-year horizon. Its ‘hope and a future’ therefore cannot mean that every individual plan will quickly prosper. Jeremiah has just told the people to build homes and seek their neighbours’ good while they wait. Christian hope similarly sustains through abandonment and opens towards charity. God’s faithfulness gives this long, ordinary work a future; the verse is larger and more demanding than a guarantee of personal success.

CCC 1818.

This difficult judgement speech must be read with verse 31, which condemns the people’s sacrifice of their children as pollution. It cannot make child killing a holy command. Irenaeus read the troubling “statutes” through God’s corrective response to rebellion, insisting that both covenants come from the same God. That is an early Christian interpretation, not an explanation of every difficulty in the passage. The governing Catholic distinction remains essential: God can judge sin and permit its consequences without becoming the author of moral evil.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.15.1; CCC 311.

Ammon’s ambition is judged by what it does to vulnerable human beings. Territorial gain cannot make atrocity acceptable. The surrounding oracles address nations beyond Israel, and the Catholic Encyclopedia observes that their guilt concerns basic humanity and good faith rather than ignorance of Israel’s God. Moral obligation therefore reaches across religious and national boundaries. The victims’ dignity does not depend on belonging to the conqueror’s people, and political success cannot turn their destruction into justice.

CE, “Amos”.

Jesus calls for speech that can be trusted without multiplying religious guarantees. Catholic tradition does not understand this as excluding every solemn oath: the Catechism allows oaths for grave and just reasons, such as truthful testimony in court. Invoking God must serve truth and justice. It cannot make deceit acceptable or replace the ordinary integrity expressed in a reliable yes or no.

CCC 2154

Jesus teaches us to ask the Father for protection from the path into sin. The Catechism explains this petition as asking not to enter temptation or yield to it; God himself does not entice us to evil. We need discernment to recognise an apparent good that would harm us, and strength to refuse it. Being tempted is not already consent. This prayer places our vulnerable freedom within the care of the Father who wants to set us free.

CCC 2846–2847

phrase: his brothers James, Joses, Simon, and Judas
body:
Catholic tradition reads these brothers as close relatives, rather than other children of Mary. The Catechism points to James and Joseph as sons of another Mary named in Matthew's Passion account. This reading belongs with the Church's confession of Mary's perpetual virginity. The family language here therefore needs to be understood within the wider biblical use of kinship terms; the English word brothers alone does not settle the relationship.

CCC 499–500

Matthew describes the boy's suffering and then narrates Jesus expelling a demon. This particular account does not identify epilepsy in general with possession. Catholic teaching expressly distinguishes illness, which requires medical care, from demonic affliction, and requires careful discernment before exorcism. The father's appeal directs attention first to a suffering child who needs help. A reader should not use the story to diagnose someone else's illness as spiritual failure.

CCC 1673

phrase: May his blood be on us and on our children
body:
This cry cannot make a whole people, or later generations, guilty of Jesus' death. The Catechism explicitly rejects that conclusion: neither all Jews present then nor Jews today can be charged with the Passion's crimes. The responsibility of particular people belongs to God's judgement. Christian readers are instead called to recognise their own sins within the human need for redemption. The passage must never become a warrant for hostility towards Jewish people.

CCC 597–598

phrase: if they drink any deadly thing
body:
The promised signs accompany the mission; they are not instructions to manufacture danger. Acts describes Paul surviving a snakebite while gathering firewood, not seeking one as a demonstration. Catholic teaching calls attempts to force God's protection a form of testing him. This promise therefore offers confidence in God's saving power, never a reason to drink poison, handle dangerous snakes or judge someone's faith by their survival.

CCC 2119

phrase: blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it
body:
Jesus directs praise from physical motherhood to hearing and keeping God's word. Mary herself exemplifies that deeper blessedness: she believes the promise and receives it in obedient faith. The Catechism quotes Augustine's striking judgement that she is more blessed for embracing faith in Christ than for conceiving his flesh. Her maternity is unique, but the faith that makes her a disciple opens a path others can share.

CCC 506

Peter explicitly says that the property and its proceeds were theirs to dispose of. Chrysostom stresses this freedom: the apostles had compelled neither the sale nor the donation. The wrong is the deliberate deception presented as a holy gift, which he reads as sacrilege. Luke's severe judgement scene exposes a threat to the community from within: an appearance of generosity can conceal a divided heart. Giving serves communion only when it is truthful.

Chrysostom, Acts 12

phrase: Let’s do evil, that good may come
body:
Paul rejects a conclusion falsely drawn from his teaching about grace: if God can bring good from sin, we may commit sin to help the outcome. The Catechism states the principle directly: we may not do evil so that good results. A worthy purpose matters, but so does what we actually choose to do. God's ability to redeem wrongdoing gives us hope for repair; it does not turn wrongdoing into a legitimate tool.

CCC 1755–1756

Chrysostom warns against stretching this image beyond its purpose. The potter illustrates God's sovereignty and a wisdom we cannot fully judge; it does not make human beings morally passive clay. If God simply manufactured good and evil choices, he observes, responsibility would disappear. The following appeal to God's patience also matters. In this patristic reading, Paul calls for humility before divine mercy without abolishing the freedom by which people respond to it.

Chrysostom, Romans 16

These greetings preserve people whose work could otherwise disappear behind Paul's more familiar name. Chrysostom reads Junia as a woman and marvels that her devotion won the title of apostle. He also praises Paul's willingness to acknowledge believers who preceded him in Christ. The greeting does not describe Junia's precise duties, but it records recognised courage and service. Reading the names attentively reveals a mission sustained by many people, including women whom the apostle publicly honours.

Chrysostom, Romans 31

phrase: the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body
body:
Paul makes the obligation reciprocal: each spouse owes loving care to the other. The Catechism grounds marriage in equal personal dignity and mutual, unreserved affection. Bodily self-giving belongs within that relationship of persons; it cannot become a right to coercion. Catholic teaching calls forcible violation of sexual intimacy intrinsically evil. The passage asks spouses to relinquish selfishness and attend to each other's good, rather than granting one person ownership of another.

CCC 1645 · CCC 2356

phrase: your faith also is in vain
body:
Paul stakes the Gospel on God's act of raising Jesus. An inspiring memory of a dead teacher would not be enough: without resurrection, he says, faith is empty and sin still holds humanity. The Catechism therefore calls the Resurrection the confirmation of Christ's works and teaching. Christian hope concerns something God has done, opening a future we could not manufacture by conviction alone. The announcement comes before the courage it gives.

CCC 651

phrase: he made to be sin on our behalf
body:
Paul begins by affirming that Christ knew no sin. Made to be sin therefore cannot mean that Jesus became personally guilty of wrongdoing. The Catechism explains that he entered our condition of estrangement in redeeming love, establishing solidarity with sinners. His self-offering reaches the place from which we need rescue while remaining the act of the sinless Son. The purpose is transformation: through him we are brought into God's righteousness.

CCC 602–603

phrase: the flesh lusts against the Spirit
body:
Flesh here cannot simply mean the body: Paul's list includes jealousy, rivalry and division as well as bodily appetites. The Catechism explains that the contrast concerns resistance or openness to the Holy Spirit, rather than contempt for our embodied nature. A person can be governed by pride while pursuing apparently spiritual things. Life in the Spirit instead bears fruit in the whole person, including bodily conduct, relationships and habits of thought.

CCC 2515–2516

This difficult sentence ends with perseverance in faith, love and holiness. It cannot make childbirth an independent means of salvation or exclude women who have no children. Catholic teaching honours both marriage and consecrated virginity as gifts from Christ, while affirming that no one earns the initial grace of salvation. The phrase's precise interpretation requires care; its place within this letter must remain consistent with the one mediator who gave himself for all and the grace that calls every person to holiness.

CCC 1618–1620 · CCC 2010

phrase: he has become guilty of all
body:
James refuses to let obedience in one area excuse injustice in another. The next verse points to the same God who commands both fidelity and respect for life. The Catechism calls the commandments an organic unity: love of God and neighbour cannot be pulled apart. That does not make every sin equally grave. Catholic teaching also distinguishes mortal from venial sin. The challenge is to receive God's law as a whole, rather than use selected virtues to shelter a chosen wrong.

CCC 2069 · CCC 1854

John has already warned that claiming to have no sin is self-deception and named Christ as advocate when believers fall. Here his uncompromising language expresses the incompatibility of sin with the life received from God. Baptism does not make a Christian incapable of wrongdoing: the Catechism explicitly says human weakness and the inclination to sin remain. New birth calls us into an ongoing struggle for holiness, with grace and repentance, rather than a claim of personal immunity from failure.

CCC 1425–1426

Augustine reads the first resurrection as passing from the death of sin into renewed life now, while awaiting the future resurrection of the body. He understands the saints' reign as already beginning in the Church, among living believers and those who have died in Christ. One interpretation he offers of the thousand years is the whole present age, expressed by a number of fullness. This influential reading directs attention to sharing Christ's life today. Catholic teaching also rejects identifying the final kingdom with an earthly political achievement.

Augustine, City of God 20.7–9 · CCC 676
